German Chancellor Immediately Calls for Sweeping Reforms Divide and conquer? By Terrina Jairaj Sep 7th, 2026, 11:45 pm Save us as a preferred source in Google Share Share Share The political landscape in Germany has been rocked by a historic election result in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the far-right Alternative for Germany, or AfD (Alternative für Deutschland), secured a commanding victory that has sent shockwaves through the European Union. According to the Daily Mail , the result, which saw the AfD capture 43.8% of the vote, has left Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), in a state of disarray. The CDU, which leads the national ruling coalition, managed only 17.2% of the vote in this regional contest. For Merz, who has been grappling with low popularity ratings and a sluggish economy, the loss is nothing short of catastrophic. At a press conference held on September 8, 2026, a day after the vote, a crestfallen Merz admitted he was deeply shocked by the outcome. He described the result as the heaviest electoral defeat his party has suffered in decades, and he acknowledged that the situation necessitates immediate consequences for his government. Despite the pressure, Merz is doubling down on his agenda He stated that giving up is not an option for him, and he remains determined to push through fundamental reforms to the German economy, including changes to the pension system. He maintains that these moves are essential for the future of the country and the opportunities of the next generation. However, he also recognized the need to justify these potentially painful reforms in a way that resonates with voters both rationally and emotionally. Funny how the only parties in all countries to save us are all Israel supporters. Is this how they’re infiltrating our governments? Causing destruction and then forcing us to vote them in? Why aren’t we allowed a party anywhere who just supports their own and that’s it? Weird! — Cheryl??? (@Woman10101) September 6, 2026 Merz was quick to reassure international allies that Germany’s institutions remain resilient and that the country will continue to uphold its values and its firm stance against Russia. According to the Associated Press , he vowed that he would not budge one millimeter from his conviction that Germany must defend its freedom. The AfD’s success is a landmark moment, as it brings a far-right party closer to leading a German government than at any point since the Second World War. The surge in support is widely attributed to deep-seated economic frustrations that have lingered since the 1990 reunification, as well as a strong sense of nostalgia for life in the former communist East Germany. The party’s platform is explicitly anti-immigration and Russia-friendly, with promises to close borders, deport those without residency permits, and halt state funding for integration programs. They have also proposed mandatory work for asylum-seekers and have drawn significant controversy for their language regarding the Bauhaus school of design, which critics argue mirrors rhetoric used by the Nazis. Many high-profile figures across the globe celebrated the win Tech billionaire Elon Musk stated, “Well done!” following the results. The AfD’s lead candidate in the state, Ulrich Siegmund, was quick to reply, thanking Musk for his support and his clear perspective on modern political developments. Mediaite reports that Siegmund expressed a strong desire for cooperation, suggesting that Germany could become a place worth investing in once again under their leadership. Thank you, @elonmusk , for your support and for your clear and highly important perspective on the political developments of our time — including here in Germany. If we take responsibility here, I would very much welcome the opportunity for strong and constructive cooperation.… — Ulrich Siegmund (@UlrichSiegmund) September 6, 2026 Meanwhile, President Donald Trump amplified the news by posting a screenshot of the election projection on Truth Social without adding a comment. Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev also shared the image, hailing the result as a historic win for the pragmatic AfD. Not everyone is celebrating, however. EU leaders are in a state of panic, and there is growing concern about the potential ripple effects across the continent. France’s Emmanuel Macron has seen his allies call for a broad coalition to keep the hard right out of power. Clement Beaune and Philippe Grangeon, two loyalists close to the French president, argued in a joint text that no one will win or govern alone in 2027. They urged moderate political factions to unite before the presidential election rather than improvising a coalition in the heat of the moment. Beaune wrote that we can see it once more in Germany, where the far right is on the threshold of power, and insisted that we cannot carry on as before. The atmosphere in Poland and Spain has been equally tense Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk issued a sharp rebuke, stating that in Poland, only idiots or traitors could rejoice at the AfD triumph. Similarly, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez warned that an extremist threat is advancing across the globe. Within Germany, the path forward for the AfD remains complex. While they won by a wide margin, they fell three seats short of the 42 needed for an absolute majority in the 83-member parliament. Other mainstream parties have maintained a so-called firewall, refusing to enter a coalition with the AfD, which has been designated as a suspected extremist group by German intelligence. Leave it to Trump to celebrate the victory of a far-right German party that shows sympathy for the Nazis, downplays the Holocaust, and flirts with Putin. https://t.co/EprgxZQ72q — Kenneth Roth (@KenRoth) September 7, 2026 Siegmund has insisted that his party has a clear mandate to govern and has rejected the idea of a minority government. The AfD is now looking at potential paths to power, including reaching out to individual lawmakers or the hard-left BSW party, which also holds a Russia-friendly stance. As Germany approaches two more regional elections on September 20 in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the pressure on the national government to respond to this populist wave is reaching a breaking point. Alice Weidel, the AfD co-founder, has already predicted that the current chancellor will be replaced before Christmas, adding another layer of uncertainty to an already volatile political environment. For now, the nation remains divided, waiting to see how these tricky negotiations will unfold. (Featured image: Steffen Prößdorf) Have a tip we should know? Elias with illustrations by Hector Borlasca; Oakland, California: Tiny Torch Books, an imprint of The Collective Book Studio; (c) 2026; ISBN 9781685-55085; 32 pages; $24.95; Publication Date: November 17, 2026. By Donald H. Harrison in San Diego Chelm is a real town in Poland often mixed up with the fictional Chelm in Jewish folklore where the people pride themselves on being wise, but they actually are naive and gullible. Stories about their foolishness are a mainstay of Jewish folklore. In this story, Chanukah is a day away when a bearded postman delivers a letter from the chief rabbi who writes that he is coming to Chelm tomorrow to celebrate Purim. Because Rabbi Velvel, the local religious authority, declares that the chief rabbi can’t possibly be wrong, the townspeople switch to preparations for Purim — costumes are brought out from closets; groggers are tested for their ability to drown out the name of “Haman” when the Megillah is read; and hamantaschen replace latkes on the community’s menu. The postman mentions that he has been travelling a long time–so long that his formerly whisker-less face now boasts a beard that reaches down to his boots. This is a clear tip off that the letter is woefully out of date, but Her Honor the Mayor Chaya doesn’t bother to investigate the matter further. Only two children, Mushka and her brother Shmendrick, realize the truth of the matter. And they don’t say a word. The cover of the book shows why. They get to eat latkes and hamantaschen on a single occasion! Chelm stories teach lessons. It turned out that the chief rabbi had written the letter ten months earlier. In this tale, a clear message is “don’t be misled by popular opinion, not if you know otherwise.” * Donald H. Harrison is publisher and editor of San Diego Jewish World . https://www.politico.eu/article/europe-c.text: ANTALYA, Turkey — European governments will hold crunch talks with China this week, in a last-ditch bid to preserve the role of scientific advice in global climate summits. On the sidelines of the U.N. climate conference in Turkey’s Antalya, senior officials from several European delegations are meeting with their Chinese counterparts to get Beijing onside in a messy fight over scientific reports, five negotiators told POLITICO. “There’s a big diplomatic move,” said Francesco Corvaro, Italy’s climate envoy. “We’re working to create pressure.” Advertisement Advertisement The dispute ensnares the U.N.’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, a body which produces scientific assessments every five to seven years, and whose advice is considered the ultimate authority on the state of knowledge on global warming — and how to fight it. The IPCC’s scientists hope to release their next series of reports in 2028. But the timeline is set by consensus among world governments, and a small group of countries led by India and Saudi Arabia are seeking to postpone publication. As part of the dispute, they’re also blocking the body’s budget, throwing the IPCC into a funding crisis that could impede its work. Any delay to the next reports would deprive climate negotiators of fresh scientific input at the pivotal COP conference in 2028, when countries must assess their progress toward the Paris Agreement and take remedial action to fix shortfalls. (The exercise is known as the second global stocktake, or GST2). “We have this issue with the IPCC — the alliance of Saudi Arabia and India that wants to postpone the reports,” said Corvaro. “Without the reports of the IPCC, it’s tough to have a good global stocktake. We need to know the details of how far we’re falling short if we want to respond.” European countries see China as key to resolving the impasse. If they manage to pull Beijing onside, the diplomats said, the blocking countries may fold. Advertisement Advertisement Finding time The IPCC is due to publish three reports. The first will focus on the science, the second on how to prepare for the effects of climate change, and the third on how to ensure warming doesn’t get worse. The latter in particular is key for the global stocktake. Most countries want the body to deliver its reports in 2028, so that the stocktake at COP33 can draw on the latest scientific research. “It is essential that the IPCC continues its work and that the seventh assessment report can be delivered in good time to inform GST2,” EU chief negotiator Diana Acconcia told reporters last week. “Europe stands on the side of science.” But India and Saudi Arabia want more time, arguing this will allow authors and governments from developing countries to review and approve the reports. “You have to give adequate time” to developing countries’ scientists, said an official from a developing country opposing the 2028 timeline. “It’s more of a principled position … not to stonewall or delay any studies.” The official spoke on condition his country not be identified. Countries pushing for the 2028 timeline — which include not only European governments but many developing countries highly vulnerable to climate change — disagree. Advertisement Advertisement “We have seen efforts to undermine the IPCC and to block its reports informing the next global stocktake,” said Marshall Islands President Hilda Heine last week. “Our Pacific scientists tell us the work can and should be completed on time.” The leaders of Norway and Brazil also backed the IPCC’s role in their speeches in Antalya last week. A French official told reporters that the Indian and Saudi Arabian efforts are “absolutely unacceptable because, in a way, it’s questioning science.” India and Saudi Arabia have suggested an alternate timeline that would deliver the first, science-only report in time for the stocktake — but push the other two, which focus on actions for countries to take, out to 2029. The process is highly political. The last stocktake, in 2023, produced a hard-fought decision signed by all governments to transition away from fossil fuels — the first time the need to do so was acknowledged in a conference decision. Saudi Arabia has since sought to walk back that outcome. This time, the timeline debate has also dragged in questions about IPCC funding, which is already under pressure due to the exit of the United States. Without a budget, the body’s work cannot continue. The result is a diplomatic deadlock over what used to be a technical detail. Advertisement Advertisement For six consecutive meetings, the IPCC’s assembly has failed to reach an agreement. Last month’s gathering in Ethiopia was suspended without result. Countries are due to meet again on Dec. 1. — the final chance to settle on a budget for the coming year. “It’s not blocking,” the developing country official insisted. “A consensus has to be found. You can’t pass the budget in a non-transparent way.” India and Saudi Arabia also have the backing of Kenya and Russia, and diplomats say China has also objected to a fast publication timeline. But they believe that Beijing can be swayed. “China is in the middle — not completely aligned with Saudi Arabia and India,” said Corvaro. “We hope it’s possible to get a common understanding with them to underline the importance of science and data.” 'Everything is polarized' As the Antalya summit brings together ministers from across the world, countries are hopeful the dispute could be resolved this week. But the stakes are high. “We have an opportunity here to get consensus on the IPCC with ministers here,” said one European diplomat, who was not authorized to speak on the record. “If they manage that, I can’t see next month’s IPCC meeting fail. Otherwise, it might be doomed.” Advertisement Advertisement Countries are mindful about not dragging the IPCC into a political debate at the COP — the two bodies fall under separate U.N. procedures — but say finding a resolution is a matter of urgency. “We have to be careful here. We don’t want to make things more difficult for the IPCC,” said a second European diplomat. “But if they don’t agree on a budget in December, it will delay and disrupt work on the next reports. That’s unacceptable.” The governments of India and Saudi Arabia did not respond to requests for comment. The developing country official said his country would oppose any attempt to address the IPCC issue in the Antalya summit’s decision text. A first draft of the final conference decision , released Monday, suggests countries note the “importance of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change for the global stocktake.” The IPCC, for its part, has welcomed government talks in Antalya. “I think governments talking here in this space [at COP] is extremely helpful,” said IPCC Vice Chair Diana Ürge-Vorsatz. “It’s crucial that we have a decision very soon, because it's very difficult for the scientists involved, it's difficult for the institution. It's very difficult for everyone to be in this uncertainty.” Advertisement The fact that the IPCC’s bureaucratic procedures had become so political was “difficult to watch,” she added. “Why has it become polarized? Because, unfortunately, at the moment everything is polarized. And because there are some parties that are trying to undermine what science is telling us, because they don't want to do what it takes to address climate change,” said Acconcia, the EU negotiator. The bloc would strive for a resolution in Antalya, she added. “We will fight for this outcome to be there.”
